Some narrative reports were suggestive of phenomena whose performance characteristics exceed the known state-of-the-art within a given domain. No technical data accompanied these reports. If validated, the attendant phenomena underlying these reports may represent a currently unmitigated threat vector.'

Section F (p. 9): 'AARO received 50 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding unmanned aerial systems (UAS) incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons, and launch sites, a 177.8 percent increase over the 18 reported in AARO's FY 2024 annual report. None of these incidents were reported as UAP.' Of the 50, '33 of 50 (66 percent) ... involved one UAS, with the other 17 involving between 2 and 7 UAS. Most cases - 47 of the 50 - occurred between 1700 and 0500 local time.' Five persisted at least an hour, 'with the longest recorded at approximately three hours.'

Section H (p. 9): 'To date, AARO has not received a UAP report in which a reporter described sustaining adverse health effects associated with their experience. However, AARO will document any UAP-related health effects, should they be reported.'

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY on satellite-flaring resolutions. The Executive Summary (p. 2) states: 'During the reporting period, AARO onboarded a new capability that enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring.' Section C, 'Notable Trends Regarding Prosaic Objects' (p. 8), states: 'AARO resolved 44 UAP-related events as attributable to satellite flaring during the reporting period.' The two figures - 238 and 44 - are not reconciled anywhere in the document.

The 238 vs 44 satellite-flaring discrepancy matters because 238 exceeds the 284 in-period reports the FY2025 report says AARO received; if 238 in-period cases were resolved as satellite flaring the residual unexplained set would be near-negligible, whereas the Section C figure of 44 leaves a far larger residual. The report's headline resolution rate cannot be reconstructed from its own published numbers. Reasoning: arithmetic comparison of the Executive Summary, Section III caseload and Section C figures within a single document.

desc: The FY2025 report covers 2 June 2024 to 30 May 2025 and reached the public on 21 July 2026 - months past the annual cycle required by 50 U.S.C. 3373(k), a statutory compliance failure that drew no visible consequence. Document reference 26-P-0880. It records 319 new reports (284 current, 35 historical), 114 of them resolved, plus 256 previously reported cases resolved in-period for a total of 370 resolutions, all attributed to prosaic causes; nine reports were identified for further analysis and 191 transferred to the active archive. Total AARO holdings: 1,870. It reports 50 unmanned aerial system notifications near nuclear infrastructure, up from 18 in the prior period - a near-tripling of drone activity over nuclear sites that the report does not resolve. It reports 262 individuals contacting AARO through the secure mechanism, of whom 255 were deemed out of scope and 7 identified for follow-up interviews. It states that no evidence suggests a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. And it carries the single most striking unresolved case AARO has published: approximately 100 airborne UAP and two likely uncrewed surface systems observed by US Navy assets off the coast of Virginia - the report's only maritime-domain case - still under active investigation, with AARO stating that a lack of timely and actionable sensor data continues to constrain its ability to resolve cases. The report also touts an expanded capability to identify satellite flares: 42 of 44 space-domain reports came from FAA pilot reports and were modelled as reflected sunlight.

claims.text: The report is titled "Fiscal Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena," is issued under "Department of War / All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office" letterhead, carries clearance number 26-P-0880, states an information cut-off of 30 May 2025, and runs 14 pages.

AARO reports receiving 319 UAP reports between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025 (284 in-period, 35 from events between 2010 and 2024), resolving 114 of them plus 256 cases from prior periods for 370 total resolutions, with case holdings of 1,870 reports as of 30 May 2025.

The report states in §IV.C that "AARO resolved 44 UAP-related events as attributable to satellite flaring during the reporting period," while §VI and the Executive Summary state that a new capability "enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring" — an unexplained discrepancy within a 14-page document.

AARO states: "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG. AARO's development process draws on established USG capabilities and operating procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel."

AARO asserts it "is authorized by law to receive all UAP-related information, including any classified national security information involving military or intelligence related activities, at any level of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs," and that "generally, no restrictions, including non-disclosure agreements, prevent AARO from receiving UAP-related information."

Between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025, 262 individuals contacted AARO through the secure reporting mechanism for persons claiming first-hand knowledge of a USG UAP-related program or activity dating back to 1945; AARO determined 255 were out of scope and identified 7 warranting a follow-on interview request.

On reports near national security sites the report states: "Some narrative reports were suggestive of phenomena whose performance characteristics exceed the known state-of-the-art within a given domain. No technical data accompanied these reports. If validated, the attendant phenomena underlying these reports may represent a currently unmitigated threat vector."

The single maritime-domain case of the reporting period was a report from U.S. Navy assets operating off the coast of Virginia describing "approximately 100 airborne UAP and two, likely uncrewed, surface systems"; AARO states it "is actively investigating this event in coordination with the reporting unit."

AARO received 50 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding UAS incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites — a 177.8 percent increase over the 18 reported in FY2024 — and states "None of these incidents were reported as UAP." Forty-seven of 50 occurred between 1700 and 0500 local time; five persisted at least an hour, the longest about three hours.

AARO transferred 191 of the 319 reports to its "active archive" for insufficient data, and identified nine reports meriting further analysis by intelligence community and science-and-technology partners.

None of AARO's 44 space-domain case assessments originated from space-based sensors: 42 came from civilian pilot reports via the FAA and two from ground-based U.S. Space Command sensors. FAA reports from civilian aviators constituted 21 percent of AARO's incoming reporting.

The report's sole named foreign-partner engagement for the year is that "AARO's deputy director presented a mission briefing to the Defense Geospatial Intelligence conference in London, United Kingdom." AARO states it "aims to fully implement the Joint Staff's classified UAP GENADMIN from February 2025."
The report was released on 21 July 2026, well after the statutory annual cycle; the FY2024 report was published in November 2024, and the FY2024 report documented 757 reports against FY2025's 319.

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who created AARO in the FY2022 NDAA and secured FY2024 NDAA language requiring declassification of UAP records, issued a same-day statement on 21 July 2026 calling the report "another crucial step forward," describing AARO as "the most comprehensive government effort on UAPs to date," and characterizing the numbers as 319 received and 114 explained, "leaving 205 unresolved."

dossier.denialPosture: The report issues two categorical denials and one implicit one. On materials: "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials." On health: "To date, AARO has not received a UAP report in which a reporter described sustaining adverse health effects." On adversary technology: "None of the cases AARO resolved indicate advanced foreign adversarial capabilities or breakthrough technologies in any domain." Each is scoped to what has reached AARO rather than to what exists, and each is undercut within the same document by the unmitigated-threat-vector language, the hundred-object Virginia maritime case, and the fact that AARO is building a materials custody process for materials it says do not exist.
dossier.narrative:
The arithmetic is the place to start, because the report's own numbers do not reconcile cleanly and the discrepancy runs through its most-promoted achievement. AARO received 319 reports between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025: 284 events inside the window and 35 from 2010 to 2024 not previously reported. Of the 319, AARO resolved 114 and additionally resolved 256 cases from prior periods, for 370 resolutions in the reporting period. Case holdings totaled 1,870 as of 30 May 2025. By domain, 274 were airborne, 44 space, one maritime. Of the 319, 191 were transferred to the "active archive" — the category for cases with insufficient data to assess whether performance characteristics are consistent with natural phenomena or exceed the known state of the art. Nine reports were identified as meriting further analysis by intelligence community and science-and-technology partners. Two case files were merged.

Now the flaring numbers. Section III.A states that all 44 space-domain reports were assessed as satellite flaring, of which 42 came from FAA civilian pilot reports and two from ground-based U.S. Space Command sensors — and notes, pointedly, that "none of AARO's space-domain case assessments originated from space-based sensors." Section IV.C states: "AARO resolved 44 UAP-related events as attributable to satellite flaring during the reporting period." Section VI states: "This capability, consisting of advanced three-dimensional modeling and simulation applications, enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring." The executive summary uses 238. Gillibrand's press release uses 238. The 238 figure only coheres if it spans the 256 previously reported cases as well as the current-period 44, which the report never states and which would mean the office's flagship analytic advance was applied overwhelmingly to a backlog rather than to new reporting. A downstream analyst should treat the 238/44 gap as an unresolved presentation problem in a fourteen-page document.

The substantive denials come in Section IV.G and Section IV.H. On materials: "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG. AARO's development process draws on established USG capabilities and operating procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel." On health: "To date, AARO has not received a UAP report in which a reporter described sustaining adverse health effects associated with their experience." Both are negative claims about AARO's own holdings, not about the world. The report never asserts that no such program or materials exist; it asserts that no evidence of them has reached this office.

The access claim in Section V.C is the report's strongest institutional assertion and its most testable: "AARO is authorized by law to receive all UAP-related information, including any classified national security information involving military or intelligence related activities, at any level of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs. Generally, no restrictions, including non-disclosure agreements, prevent AARO from receiving UAP-related information, regardless of the organizational affiliation of the original classification authority within the DoW, the IC, or any other USG department or agency." Note the hedge: "Generally." Note also what the sentence does not say — it describes a right to receive, not an exercised capability to compel, and it does not state that AARO has audited any carved-out special access program. Against that, 262 individuals used the secure reporting mechanism in the period; AARO determined 255 were out of scope and identified seven for follow-on interview. A 97 percent out-of-scope rate is either an accurate measure of noise or a measure of a scoping filter, and the report gives no criteria by which to tell.

Two passages cut against the report's own framing. Section IV.E: "AARO received and analyzed several reports describing UAP in or near national security sites or critical infrastructure. Some narrative reports were suggestive of phenomena whose performance characteristics exceed the known state-of-the-art within a given domain. No technical data accompanied these reports. If validated, the attendant phenomena underlying these reports may represent a currently unmitigated threat vector." And Section III.A, the sole maritime case: a report from U.S. Navy assets operating off the coast of Virginia describing "approximately 100 airborne UAP and two, likely uncrewed, surface systems," which AARO says it is actively investigating. An office reporting no flight-safety concerns and no anomalous residue is simultaneously reporting an unmitigated threat vector and a hundred-object maritime event under investigation.

Section IV.F is the nuclear line. AARO received 50 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding unmanned aerial system incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites — a 177.8 percent increase over the 18 in the FY2024 report. "None of these incidents were reported as UAP." Forty-seven of the 50 occurred between 1700 and 0500 local; five persisted at least an hour, the longest about three hours; 33 involved a single system, 17 involved between two and seven. The categorical exclusion of all 50 from UAP status is a classification decision made by the reporting agencies, not an analytic finding by AARO, and the report does not say who made it.

On process: the report was released 21 July 2026 under a statute requiring submission "not later than 180 days after December 23, 2022, and annually thereafter for four years." The FY2024 report was published in November 2024 and documented 757 reports against FY2025's 319. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who created AARO in the FY2022 NDAA and secured the FY2024 NDAA declassification language, issued a same-day statement calling the report "another crucial step forward" and AARO "the most comprehensive government effort on UAPs to date," and framed the arithmetic as 319 received, 114 explained, "leaving 205 unresolved." The report's own foreign-engagement section names exactly one activity for the year: AARO's deputy director presented a mission briefing to the Defense Geospatial Intelligence conference in London.
openQuestions: Why does §IV.C state 44 satellite-flaring resolutions for the reporting period while §VI and the Executive Summary state 238? The report never reconciles the figures or states which case population the 238 spans.
Who decided that all 50 nuclear-adjacent UAS incidents were "not reported as UAP" — the reporting agencies or AARO — and against what criteria?
What are the scoping criteria by which 255 of 262 first-hand claimants were ruled out of scope? None are published.
AARO says it is building a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials "by an appropriate line organization." Which organization, under what authority, and with what facility?
AARO claims access regardless of special access controls. Has AARO ever invoked that authority against a specific carved-out SAP, and if so, was access granted or refused?
The February 2025 Joint Staff UAP GENADMIN remains classified. What does it direct, and does it reach contractor personnel?
The Virginia maritime case describes approximately 100 airborne UAP and two likely uncrewed surface systems. What sensors recorded it, and what is the current status of the investigation?

Two reports described electronic or avionic interference near operational aircraft; AARO says it has "not yet rendered a determination." What is the determination timeline, and which airframes were involved?
The report was released roughly eight months later than the prior year's. What accounts for the delay, and was the report submitted to Congress on time even if released late?
dossier.whatItIs: The Fiscal Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena is the fourteen-page statutory report submitted by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office under 50 U.S.C. § 3373(k), covering UAP events from 2 June 2024 to 30 May 2025, bearing the clearance number 26-P-0880 and issued under the letterhead "Department of War." It was publicly released on 21 July 2026, months after the annual reporting cycle Congress contemplated. It records 319 new reports, 370 total resolutions, and no unexplained residue attributed to advanced foreign or non-human capability.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the current, dated instrument of official denial, and it is therefore the most useful single artifact on the board. Its flat assertion — "To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials" — is immediately followed by the statement that AARO "is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG," a process AARO says draws on established procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel. An office that has found nothing is building a custody chain for it. The report also claims an access authority that collides directly with standing DoD regulation: AARO states it is authorized to receive UAP information "regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs," while DoDD 5205.07 §3.2.g simultaneously forbids any DoD contractor employee from providing SAP material to Congress without SAPCO approval and 32 CFR 117.6 removes DCSA visibility from carved-out programs entirely. Claiming access is not the same as exercising it. And the report is internally inconsistent on its headline finding: §IV.C states AARO resolved 44 events as satellite flaring during the reporting period while §VI states the new capability "enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring."
